item.content:encoded:
The German Institute of Development and Sustainability (IDOS) is inviting applications for a Researcher (m/f/diverse) position within its Research Department “Environmental Governance.” The position focuses on water governance, water security, water politics, environmental governance, and policy advice, particularly in low- and middle-income countries and potentially conflict-affected settings.

The opportunity is particularly suited to researchers with a background in the social sciences, sustainability science, environmental governance, political ecology, or related fields, and with demonstrated research and publication experience on water security issues.

The successful candidate will become part of the IDOS water governance team, contributing to academic research, policy advice, networking, science communication, and potentially third-party funding applications for interdisciplinary and transdisciplinary projects.

The position is based at IDOS in Bonn, Germany, is offered at 50% part-time employment equivalent to 19.5 hours per week, and is initially limited to three years, with a possible extension.

Researcher Position at IDOS: Overview

The German Institute of Development and Sustainability (IDOS) conducts research and provides policy advice at the intersection of development and sustainability. Its work aims to contribute to a cooperative and sustainable multipolar world through research, policy engagement, knowledge cooperation, and education.

For this vacancy, IDOS is seeking a researcher who can contribute to its work on water governance and water security, with a particular focus on issues affecting low- and middle-income countries.

Position details

  • Position: Researcher (m/f/diverse)
  • Position number: 2026-C-02
  • Institution: German Institute of Development and Sustainability (IDOS)
  • Research Department: Environmental Governance
  • Research area: Water governance and water security
  • Location: Bonn, Germany
  • Working time: 50% part-time
  • Weekly hours: 19.5 hours per week
  • Salary: German public sector tariff, EG13 up to EG14 TVöD Bund, depending on qualifications
  • Gross salary: Approximately €31,250–€48,000 for a 50% position
  • Start date: From 1 January 2027
  • Contract duration: Three years, with a possible option for extension
  • Potential increase in working time: The position may potentially increase to 60% in 2028 and 2029
  • Application deadline: 7 October 2026 at 23:59 CEST
  • Expected interview date: 3 November 2026

About the Research Area: Water Security

The researcher will join the IDOS water governance team and conduct research and policy advice on selected questions relating to water politics, water policies, water governance, and water security.

The work will focus particularly on low- and middle-income countries and may include settings affected by conflict or other forms of instability.

Water security is understood broadly as ensuring access to an acceptable quantity and quality of water for:

  • Human health
  • Livelihoods
  • Ecosystems
  • Economic and productive activities

It also considers the need to maintain an acceptable level of water-related risks for people, the environment, and economies.

This broad definition means that the successful researcher could work across several interconnected dimensions of water security.

Key Water Security Topics

Research under this position may address one or more of the following areas:

1. Surface and Groundwater Use

The role may examine the governance and political dimensions of surface and groundwater resources, including:

  • Overuse of water resources
  • Groundwater governance
  • Surface-water management
  • Competition over water resources
  • Institutional arrangements for water management
  • Policies governing water use
  • Environmental and social impacts of water exploitation

2. Wastewater Treatment and Reuse

The researcher may also investigate issues surrounding:

  • Wastewater treatment
  • Wastewater management
  • Reuse of treated wastewater
  • Governance of wastewater systems
  • Environmental risks
  • Policy frameworks for wastewater reuse
  • Sustainable approaches to water resource management

3. Water-Related Extreme Events

Another potential area of research involves water-related risks and extreme events, such as:

  • Flooding
  • Drought
  • Water scarcity
  • Climate-related water risks
  • Disaster risk governance
  • Institutional responses to extreme events
  • Policies for adapting to changing water-related risks

4. Access to Sanitation Services

The position may also cover questions related to:

  • Access to sanitation
  • Sanitation governance
  • Public policy
  • Inequality in access to services
  • Institutional challenges
  • Sustainable sanitation systems
  • Health and environmental implications of inadequate sanitation

5. Transboundary and Multilateral Water Relations

The researcher may conduct research on water relations that cross national borders, including:

  • Transboundary water governance
  • International water politics
  • Cooperation between countries
  • Water-related conflicts
  • Multilateral water governance
  • International institutions and agreements
  • Political dimensions of shared water resources

Main Responsibilities

The successful candidate will have responsibilities spanning research, policy advice, networking, communication, and funding development.

Conducting Academic Research

The researcher will undertake independent and collaborative research related to water security and governance.

The role requires the ability to identify important research questions, develop appropriate conceptual frameworks, conduct research, analyse findings, and communicate results to academic and policy audiences.

Research may involve studying institutional arrangements, political processes, environmental governance systems, and the relationships between different levels of government and stakeholders.

Providing Policy Advice

An important part of the position is translating research into useful knowledge for policymakers and other stakeholders.

The successful applicant should therefore be comfortable working beyond purely academic research and responding to demands for policy advice.

This could involve:

  • Developing policy-oriented research outputs
  • Communicating research findings to policymakers
  • Contributing to policy discussions
  • Responding to emerging policy questions
  • Translating complex research findings into accessible recommendations
  • Engaging with stakeholders outside academia

Supporting IDOS Networking and Positioning

The researcher will also contribute to the institute’s broader networking and positioning on water security topics.

This involves helping IDOS strengthen its profile and relationships in the field of water governance and security.

The successful applicant is expected to engage with relevant researchers, institutions, policymakers, practitioners, and other stakeholders.

Supporting Third-Party Funding Applications

The position also provides an opportunity to contribute to the development of externally funded research.

Candidates are encouraged to support third-party funding applications for inter- and transdisciplinary projects related to water security.

Experience with third-party funding acquisition is considered an advantage.

The possibility of increasing the position to 60% in 2028 and 2029 is connected to successful acquisition of third-party funding.

Required Qualifications

Applicants must demonstrate a strong academic and research background relevant to the position.

Master’s Degree

A Master’s degree is required.

The degree should preferably be in an area such as:

  • Social sciences
  • Political science
  • Economics
  • Human geography
  • Anthropology
  • Sustainability science with a social science focus
  • Another closely related field

PhD Preferred

A PhD is preferably expected, although the advertisement does not state that it is an absolute requirement.

Applicants with strong research experience and relevant publications may therefore be considered based on their overall qualifications.

Excellent Academic Performance

The position calls for candidates with excellent grades in their relevant university education.

Research Experience in Water Security

One of the most important requirements is demonstrated social science research experience in one or more of the specified water security fields.

Candidates should be able to demonstrate their research expertise through peer-reviewed academic publications, including submissions.

Relevant research areas include:

  • Surface-water governance
  • Groundwater governance
  • Water overuse
  • Wastewater treatment
  • Wastewater reuse
  • Water-related extreme events
  • Sanitation
  • Transboundary water governance
  • Multilateral water relations
  • Water politics
  • Water policy
  • Water security
  • Environmental governance
  • Political ecology

Applicants do not necessarily need to have worked across every one of these areas. Experience in at least one of the specified water security topics can be relevant.

Conceptual and Theoretical Skills

The successful candidate should have strong conceptual abilities, particularly in areas such as:

Institutional Analysis

The ability to examine how institutions shape environmental and water governance processes is important for this role.

Multi-Level Environmental Governance

Applicants should understand how water-related decisions and governance operate across different levels, potentially involving:

  • Local institutions
  • Communities
  • Municipal authorities
  • National governments
  • Regional organisations
  • International institutions
  • Other relevant stakeholders

Political Ecology

Knowledge of political ecology is also relevant, particularly for understanding the relationships between:

  • Environmental resources
  • Political power
  • Institutions
  • Communities
  • Economic interests
  • Inequality
  • Resource access

Research Methodology Requirements

The position requires experience with qualitative research methodologies in the social sciences.

Applicants should therefore be able to demonstrate familiarity with approaches used to investigate complex social, political, institutional, and environmental questions.

Mixed Methods

Experience with mixed-methods research is considered an additional asset.

Candidates who can combine qualitative approaches with quantitative data, statistical analysis, surveys, or other methods may therefore have an advantage.

Experience in Low- and Middle-Income Countries

Research or professional experience in a low- or middle-income country context is specifically required.

This is an important aspect of the position because IDOS’s work on water security focuses particularly on challenges and governance systems in such contexts.

Relevant experience could include research, fieldwork, professional work, development projects, policy work, or other substantive engagement with low- and middle-income country settings.

Policy and Science Communication Experience

The successful applicant should be willing to engage in:

  • Policy advice
  • Science communication
  • Research dissemination
  • Stakeholder engagement
  • Communication with non-academic audiences

Previous experience in policy advice or science communication is considered an advantage.

Third-Party Funding Experience

Experience with third-party funding acquisition is an asset.

Candidates who have participated in activities such as:

  • Grant proposal development
  • Research funding applications
  • Consortium development
  • Donor engagement
  • Fundraising for research projects
  • Competitive funding applications

may therefore be particularly well positioned for the role.

Interdisciplinary and Transdisciplinary Collaboration

IDOS is looking for someone who is eager to work in inter- and transdisciplinary teams.

This means the researcher should be comfortable collaborating across disciplinary boundaries and potentially working with people from academia, government, civil society, development organisations, practitioners, and other stakeholder groups.

Communication and Organisational Skills

Strong skills in the following areas are expected:

  • Academic writing
  • Policy writing
  • Professional communication
  • Organisation
  • Independent work
  • Research planning
  • Collaboration
  • Time management

The advertisement particularly emphasises the ability to work in a self-directed manner.

The researcher should also have the flexibility to respond to changing demands for policy advice.

International Travel and Tropical-Country Work

The position requires a willingness and ability to travel abroad, including to countries with tropical climates.

The advertisement specifically mentions “Tropentauglichkeit,” referring to the ability or suitability to work and travel in tropical-climate environments.

Candidates should therefore be prepared for international research or professional travel where required.

Employment Conditions and Salary

The position is offered on a 50% part-time basis, equivalent to 19.5 hours per week.

The salary follows the German public-sector pay system:

EG13 up to EG14 TVöD Bund, depending on the applicant’s qualifications.

The advertised gross salary range for the 50% position is approximately:

€31,250 to €48,000 gross

The position is initially limited to three years, beginning from January 2027, with a possible option for contract extension.

There is also an opportunity for the position to increase to 60% in 2028 and 2029, depending on successful third-party funding acquisition.

Benefits and What IDOS Offers

IDOS lists a range of employment and social benefits for the successful candidate.

Flexible Working Hours

The role provides flexible working arrangements within the 50% working-time framework.

The standard working week is:

19.5 hours per week

Mobile Working

The position offers the possibility of mobile working from within Germany for up to 60% of the working time per week.

At least 40% of working time per week must be spent in person in Bonn.

This means candidates should be prepared to work from the IDOS workplace in Bonn for the required proportion of their working time.

Public Transportation Benefits

Employees can make use of a subsidised Deutschland-Job-Ticket, supporting access to public transportation.

The institute also highlights good access to public transport.

Special Annual Payment

Employees receive a special annual payment in accordance with the TVöD Bund collective agreement for the German federal government.

Annual Leave

The position includes:

  • Up to 30 days of annual vacation
  • An additional 6 days of company vacation

Professional Development

IDOS offers training opportunities intended to support employees’ continuing professional development.

These may help researchers strengthen their academic, professional, methodological, and organisational skills.

Pension Scheme

The employer contributes to the company pension scheme through VBLU.

Additional Benefits

IDOS also notes that employees can receive additional social and monetary benefits beyond those specifically listed in the vacancy announcement.

Diversity and Equal Opportunity

IDOS explicitly states that it actively promotes equality between women and men and diversity within the institute.

The organisation welcomes applications from people of different backgrounds and explicitly states that it welcomes:

  • People of colour
  • People of all nationalities
  • People of all religions and beliefs
  • People of different sexual orientations
  • People of all gender identities
  • People across all age groups
  • People with disabilities
  • People with a family migration history

Therefore, the vacancy is not limited to applicants from Germany or Europe on the basis of nationality.

Qualified applicants from Africa, Asia, Europe, the Americas, the Middle East, Oceania, and other regions can apply, provided they meet the academic, research, professional, and other requirements of the position.

Recognition of Foreign University Degrees

Applicants who obtained their university degree outside Germany have an additional documentation requirement.

They should attach the relevant Anabin database excerpt to their application documents as evidence of recognition of the foreign degree by the Central Office for Foreign Education (ZAB) of the Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education and Cultural Affairs (KMK).

International applicants should therefore pay particular attention to this requirement before submitting their applications.

Who Should Apply?

This opportunity is particularly relevant for researchers who have a combination of:

  1. A Master’s degree or preferably a PhD in a relevant social science or sustainability field.
  2. Strong academic performance.
  3. Research experience related to water security.
  4. Peer-reviewed publications or submissions demonstrating relevant research experience.
  5. Experience with qualitative social science research.
  6. Research or professional experience in a low- or middle-income country.
  7. Knowledge of institutional analysis, environmental governance, or political ecology.
  8. An interest in water politics, water policy, and water governance.
  9. Strong academic and professional writing skills.
  10. An interest in policy advice and science communication.
  11. An ability to work independently.
  12. An interest in interdisciplinary and transdisciplinary research.
  13. Willingness to travel internationally, including to tropical countries.

Experience with mixed methods and third-party research funding is an additional advantage.

Application Requirements

Applicants must submit their application through the IDOS application portal.

Applications must include the following documents:

1. Cover Letter

A cover letter outlining the candidate’s:

  • Motivation for applying
  • Interest in the position
  • Relevant qualifications
  • Research background
  • Suitability for the water governance team

2. Curriculum Vitae

The CV should include:

  • Academic background
  • Professional experience
  • Research experience
  • Relevant skills
  • Publications
  • Other relevant qualifications

The CV should contain a full publication list.

Applicants should also provide their relevant academic certificates.

3. Employment References

German employment letters, known as Arbeitszeugnisse, should be provided where available.

4. Two Letters of Reference

Applicants should also provide two letters of reference, preferably together with the application.

If this is not possible at the application stage, shortlisted candidates may be permitted to submit the reference letters at a later stage.

File Submission Requirements

There are specific restrictions on the number and format of files that can be uploaded.

Applicants should note that:

  • A maximum of 4 files can be attached.
  • All files must be submitted in PDF format.
  • Each file can have a maximum size of 10 MB.

Applicants should therefore organise their documents carefully so that all required materials can be submitted within the four-file limit.

Why This Opportunity May Be Valuable for Researchers

This IDOS position provides an opportunity to combine academic research with policy engagement.

Unlike a position focused exclusively on academic publication, the role brings together several dimensions of research and development work, including:

  • Water security research
  • Environmental governance
  • Water politics
  • Policy advice
  • Science communication
  • International research
  • Networking
  • Interdisciplinary collaboration
  • Third-party funding development

The position may be particularly attractive to researchers interested in understanding how water-related challenges are shaped not only by environmental conditions but also by institutions, political systems, policies, power relations, and governance structures.

The focus on low- and middle-income countries also makes the position relevant for researchers whose academic or professional work has involved development, sustainability, international cooperation, environmental policy, or governance challenges in these contexts.

Final Summary

The German Institute of Development and Sustainability (IDOS) is recruiting a Researcher (m/f/diverse) for its Environmental Governance Research Department, with a focus on water governance and water security.

The researcher will contribute to research and policy advice on issues including groundwater and surface-water governance, wastewater treatment and reuse, water-related extreme events, sanitation, and transboundary or multilateral water relations. The work will particularly focus on low- and middle-income countries and potentially conflict-affected settings.

The position is offered at 50% part-time employment, equivalent to 19.5 hours per week, with a salary of approximately €31,250–€48,000 gross for the 50% position, depending on qualifications and the applicable TVöD classification. The contract is initially for three years, with a possible extension and potential increase to 60% in 2028 and 2029 based on successful third-party funding acquisition.

Candidates should have a relevant Master’s degree and preferably a PhD, strong academic performance, demonstrated social science research experience in water security, relevant peer-reviewed publications, qualitative research experience, and experience in a low- or middle-income country context. Knowledge of institutional analysis, multi-level environmental governance, and political ecology is particularly relevant.

The application deadline is 7 October 2026 at 23:59 CEST, and the expected interview date is 3 November 2026.

Overall, this is a strong opportunity for an experienced social science or sustainability researcher seeking to work at the intersection of water security, environmental governance, international development, academic research, and policy advice in an internationally oriented research institution in Germany.

item.content:encoded:
Applications are now open for the Mama Cash Spark Fund 2026, a flexible grant programme supporting self-led feminist groups working for the rights of women, girls, trans people and intersex people in the Netherlands and the ABCSSS islands: Aruba, Bonaire, Curaçao, Saba, Sint Eustatius and Sint Maarten.

The Spark Fund is designed particularly for grassroots and structurally excluded communities working on urgent and contested political issues. Grants range from €5,000 to €12,000 per project and can support work for a period of up to two years. Mama Cash accepts applications from both formal organisations and informal groups, including newly established and volunteer-led initiatives that may have difficulty accessing conventional institutional funding.

The 2026 application period runs from:

20 August 2026 to 20 September 2026

The final deadline is:

20 September 2026 at 11:59 PM CEST.

Applicants can apply in several accessible formats, including:

  • Written application
  • Video application
  • Audio application

Applications can be submitted in English or Dutch. Groups that would prefer to apply in another language are encouraged to contact Mama Cash at spark@mamacash.org to discuss possible support.

The Spark Fund is especially notable because applicants do not need to be formally registered, do not need an organisational bank account, and do not need a residence permit or official identification in order to apply.

About the Mama Cash Spark Fund

Mama Cash is an international feminist fund with deep roots in feminist movements in the Netherlands.

Through the Spark Fund, the organisation honours its historical connection to the Dutch lesbian feminist activist movement while continuing to support communities working for the rights of:

  • Women
  • Girls
  • Trans people
  • Intersex people

The Fund is geographically focused on the Netherlands and the ABCSSS islands and is intended to help self-led groups pursue bold, grassroots work that challenges structural inequality.

Mama Cash describes the idea behind the programme simply:

A small amount of money can spark major, radical change.

The Fund therefore does not assume that transformative work must come from large, established NGOs.

Instead, it deliberately makes room for:

  • Informal collectives
  • New groups
  • Volunteer-led initiatives
  • Unregistered movements
  • Small organisations
  • Groups without paid staff
  • Groups without offices
  • Groups with limited access to flexible funding

This makes the Spark Fund particularly relevant to activists who may struggle to qualify for conventional institutional grants.

How Much Funding Is Available?

Successful applicants can receive between:

€5,000 and €12,000

for a project lasting:

Up to two years.

The flexibility of this range means the Fund can support relatively small grassroots initiatives as well as longer projects that need sustained support.

Importantly, the programme is not structured only around established organisations with professional fundraising departments.

Mama Cash specifically recognises that some activist groups may:

  • Be newly established
  • Operate informally
  • Lack formal organisational structures
  • Have no long-term strategic plan
  • Have limited financial infrastructure

but still have a strong idea, urgent political purpose and clear potential for structural change.

What Is the Main Purpose of the Spark Fund?

The Spark Fund supports initiatives:

By and for structurally excluded communities

that work on:

Urgent and contested issues

in the Netherlands and the ABCSSS islands.

This means the Fund is not designed primarily for neutral service-delivery programmes.

It is particularly interested in groups challenging:

  • Discrimination
  • Patriarchal systems
  • Sexism
  • Gender inequality
  • Exclusion
  • Harmful norms
  • Unequal access to rights
  • Structural barriers affecting marginalised communities

Projects should therefore have a clear political or systemic dimension.

The Four Core Eligibility Requirements

Mama Cash sets out four major eligibility criteria.

A group must:

  1. Be self-led by the women, girls, trans people and/or intersex people it serves.
  2. Work from a feminist perspective and/or focus on women’s, girls’, trans rights and/or intersex rights.
  3. Work on urgent and contested political issues in the Netherlands or the ABCSSS islands.
  4. Push for structural and systemic change.

Each of these criteria is important and deserves careful attention before submitting an application.

1. The Group Must Be Self-Led

The people whose rights are at stake must be the people who make decisions about the project.

Mama Cash gives the example of a group supporting women with disabilities.

If the project is focused on the rights of women with disabilities, then women with disabilities should themselves have meaningful leadership over:

  • Activities
  • Decision-making
  • Use of grant funds
  • Public representation

People without disabilities may participate and provide support, but they should not lead the project.

This principle is central to the Spark Fund.

Mama Cash is not simply looking for organisations that work for marginalised groups.

It prioritises groups that are genuinely led by the communities directly affected by the issues.

Why Self-Leadership Matters

The self-led requirement reflects a broader feminist grantmaking principle: people directly affected by injustice should have power over how solutions are designed.

This means a project may be less competitive if the intended beneficiaries have little influence over:

  • Strategy
  • Budget
  • Leadership
  • Project design
  • Communications

Applicants should therefore show clearly who makes decisions inside the group.

A strong application should be able to answer questions such as:

  • Who leads the group?
  • Who decides how funds are used?
  • Who determines project priorities?
  • Are the affected communities represented in leadership?
  • Who speaks publicly on behalf of the project?

2. The Group Must Work From a Feminist Perspective

Mama Cash defines feminism broadly.

The organisation understands feminist work as efforts that challenge:

  • Sexism
  • Patriarchal gender norms
  • Inequality
  • Injustice

and defend the human rights of women, girls, trans and intersex people.

The Fund recognises that gender inequality intersects with many other forms of marginalisation, including:

  • Race
  • Ethnicity
  • Sexuality
  • Class
  • Migration status
  • Disability
  • Economic status

The Spark Fund therefore supports intersectional approaches where these experiences are central to the project.

What Counts as a Feminist Project?

A project does not need to be about a traditionally defined “women’s issue.”

For example, a project about housing may qualify if it specifically addresses barriers faced by women who are:

  • Migrants
  • Queer
  • Sex workers
  • Women with disabilities
  • Rural women
  • Low-income women

The key point is that their lived experiences and rights must be central to the project rather than included only as a secondary component.

This distinction is important.

A general community housing project that happens to include some women would not automatically meet the Fund’s feminist criteria.

A project designed and led by marginalised women challenging structural barriers to safe and affordable housing may be much more aligned.

3. The Group Must Work on Urgent and Contested Political Issues

The Spark Fund is intended for groups working on issues that may be politically difficult, socially controversial or insufficiently addressed.

Mama Cash gives the example of Muslim women organising to defend their rights and express their concerns in a context where wearing the hijab, niqab or similar forms of religious covering faces criticism from government or public opinion.

Other relevant themes might potentially include:

  • Reproductive rights
  • Trans rights
  • Migrant rights
  • Disability justice
  • Sex workers’ rights
  • Racial justice
  • Religious discrimination
  • LGBTQI+ rights
  • Gender-based violence
  • Housing inequality
  • Economic exclusion

These are examples rather than a closed list.

The central requirement is that the issue is politically significant and that the project is rooted in feminist rights-based action.

4. The Project Must Push for Structural and Systemic Change

The Spark Fund is not focused only on helping individual people cope with immediate needs.

Mama Cash wants projects that also challenge the systems creating those needs.

For example, a group of migrant women might offer temporary shelter to other migrant women.

Providing shelter addresses an immediate need.

But to fit the Spark Fund’s structural-change orientation, the same group might also challenge barriers preventing migrant women from accessing:

  • Housing
  • Healthcare
  • Social services
  • Legal protection

This broader work can create benefits even for people the project cannot support directly.

What Does Structural Change Mean?

Structural change may include efforts to:

  • Change policy
  • Challenge discriminatory systems
  • Shift public attitudes
  • Improve institutional practices
  • Expand rights
  • Strengthen movement power
  • Reform harmful procedures
  • Increase representation
  • Build collective organising capacity

The project does not need to transform an entire national system within one grant period.

But it should have a credible ambition to address causes, not merely symptoms.

Who Gets Priority?

Although many eligible groups can apply, Mama Cash gives particular priority to groups facing barriers to conventional flexible funding.

These include:

  • Informal groups
  • Unregistered groups
  • Newly established groups
  • Volunteer-led groups
  • Organisations with limited organisational resources
  • Groups with no paid staff
  • Groups without office space

Mama Cash explicitly states that particular consideration is given to groups with limited organisational resources.

This is important because being a small or informal organisation is not automatically a weakness in this competition.

In fact, it may align closely with the Fund’s priorities.

Do Applicants Need to Be Registered Organisations?

No.

The Spark Fund can support:

Informal and unregistered groups.

Your group does not need to be formally registered as a Dutch foundation or other legal organisation in order to apply.

This removes an important barrier faced by grassroots movements.

Do Applicants Need an Organisational Bank Account?

No.

Mama Cash explicitly states that applicants do not need an organisational bank account to submit an application.

Groups should therefore not exclude themselves simply because they have not yet established formal banking arrangements.

If selected, Mama Cash can presumably discuss appropriate payment arrangements directly with the group.

Do Applicants Need a Residence Permit?

No.

The Spark Fund states that applicants do not need a residence permit to apply.

This can be especially important for migrant-led and undocumented communities that may otherwise be excluded from conventional grant programmes.

Do Applicants Need Official Identification?

No.

Mama Cash also states that official identification is not required simply in order to submit an application.

Together, these rules make the Fund particularly accessible to grassroots communities that may lack conventional administrative documentation.

Geographic Eligibility

The Spark Fund is geographically limited.

Projects must operate in:

  • The Netherlands
  • Aruba
  • Bonaire
  • Curaçao
  • Saba
  • Sint Eustatius
  • Sint Maarten

These islands are collectively referred to by Mama Cash as the ABCSSS islands.

The Spark Fund should therefore not be presented as a global feminist grant.

Groups based elsewhere cannot simply apply for projects in unrelated countries.

The geographic focus is specifically the Netherlands and the six named Caribbean islands.

Can Groups From the Caribbean Apply?

Yes, but only groups working in the specified territories:

  • Aruba
  • Bonaire
  • Curaçao
  • Saba
  • Sint Eustatius
  • Sint Maarten

The Fund does not automatically cover the entire Caribbean.

For example, a group based in Jamaica, Barbados or Trinidad and Tobago would not be eligible simply because it is located in the Caribbean unless it has an eligible structure or programme meeting the specific geographic criteria published by Mama Cash.

Types of Projects That May Fit the Spark Fund

Based on Mama Cash’s criteria, potentially relevant projects might include initiatives addressing:

Migrant Women’s Rights

Projects challenging structural barriers affecting migrant women’s access to housing, healthcare or legal rights.

Disability Justice

Self-led initiatives by women, girls, trans or intersex people with disabilities challenging discrimination or exclusion.

LGBTQI+ Rights

Grassroots organising around the rights and safety of queer, trans or intersex communities.

Anti-Racism and Gender Justice

Initiatives examining how racism and gender inequality intersect.

Sex Workers’ Rights

Self-led organising addressing rights, safety, legal barriers or stigma affecting sex workers.

Religious Freedom and Gender

Projects led by women affected by discrimination linked to religion, clothing or cultural identity.

Housing Rights

Feminist initiatives challenging structural housing barriers experienced by marginalised communities.

Reproductive Justice

Grassroots work defending bodily autonomy, reproductive rights or access to services.

These examples should not be interpreted as guaranteed funding areas. Projects must still meet all Spark Fund criteria.

How to Apply

The 2026 Spark Fund application window is:

20 August to 20 September 2026 at 11:59 PM CEST.

Mama Cash provides three application formats.

Option 1: Written Application

Applicants can complete the official written form online.

Written Application Form

Option 2: Video Application

Applicants who prefer to speak rather than write can submit through the video recording application.

Video Application Form

Option 3: Audio Application

Applicants can also submit an audio-recorded application.

Audio Application Form

Providing multiple formats reflects Mama Cash’s effort to make the funding process accessible to grassroots activists who may not be comfortable with traditional written grant applications.

What Languages Can Be Used?

Applications can be submitted in:

  • English
  • Dutch

Groups that would prefer another language can contact:

spark@mamacash.org

Mama Cash states that it will explore possible support or accommodations where another language would be more suitable.

How Applications Are Reviewed

Mama Cash uses a participatory grantmaking approach.

The process begins with staff reviewing applications against the Spark Fund’s:

  • Eligibility criteria
  • Priority areas

Eligible applications then move into a participatory review process involving feminist activists connected to the Mama Cash network and former Spark grantee-partners.

This means decisions are not made solely by professional grant managers detached from activist movements.

People with direct movement experience are involved in deciding which initiatives receive funding.

Who Makes the Final Decision?

According to Mama Cash’s 2026 information, final decisions are made through its participatory grantmaking structure, involving members of the Mama Cash Advisory Network and, in the detailed FAQ, a steering committee of former Spark grantee-partners drawn from feminist activist communities in the Netherlands and the ABCSSS islands.

This is consistent with Mama Cash’s broader commitment to:

Sharing power and putting decisions in the hands of activists.

When Will Applicants Hear Back?

Mama Cash states in its FAQ that grant decisions are usually announced in:

October.

Applicants should therefore monitor the contact details they provide after submission.

How to Prepare a Strong Spark Fund Application

1. Show That the Group Is Truly Self-Led

Explain clearly:

  • Who founded the group
  • Who leads it
  • Who makes decisions
  • Who controls the project budget
  • Who represents the group publicly

Do not merely state that the project “supports women.”

Show that the women, girls, trans or intersex people affected by the issue hold real power.

2. Explain the Structural Problem

A strong application should identify more than an immediate need.

Instead of saying:

“Women in our community struggle to find housing,”

explain:

  • What barriers cause the problem
  • How discrimination operates
  • Which systems reproduce inequality
  • What the group wants to change

3. Show Why the Issue Is Urgent or Contested

Explain why the issue requires action now.

For example:

  • Has policy changed?
  • Is public hostility increasing?
  • Is a community losing rights?
  • Is an overlooked group experiencing exclusion?
  • Is there a new opportunity for movement-building?

Urgency should be concrete.

4. Centre the Community’s Own Priorities

Do not design a project externally and then add marginalised communities afterward.

The people affected should be able to explain:

  • What they need
  • What they want changed
  • How they will organise
  • What success would look like

5. Explain the Feminist Dimension

Make clear how the project challenges:

  • Sexism
  • Patriarchal structures
  • Gender inequality
  • Intersectional discrimination

The feminist perspective should be integrated into the project rather than appearing only in one paragraph of the application.

6. Do Not Worry About Being a Small Group

The Fund deliberately prioritises grassroots groups.

If your initiative is:

  • Volunteer-led
  • Unregistered
  • New
  • Small
  • Without paid staff

do not hide this.

Explain how flexible funding could help the group strengthen its work.

7. Choose the Application Format That Works Best

A sophisticated written grant proposal is not automatically better than a clear video or audio submission.

Use the format that enables the group to communicate:

  • Its story
  • Its purpose
  • Its leadership
  • The problem
  • The proposed change

most effectively.

Key Information at a Glance

Fund: Mama Cash Spark Fund

Grant size: €5,000–€12,000

Funding period: Up to two years

Applications open: 20 August 2026

Deadline: 20 September 2026 at 11:59 PM CEST

Eligible locations: Netherlands, Aruba, Bonaire, Curaçao, Saba, Sint Eustatius and Sint Maarten

Target groups: Self-led groups of women, girls, trans people and/or intersex people

Formal registration required: No

Organisational bank account required to apply: No

Residence permit required: No

Official ID required to apply: No

Application formats: Written, video or audio

Application languages: English or Dutch; contact Mama Cash about other language needs

Priority applicants: Informal, newly established, volunteer-led and resource-limited groups

Selection model: Participatory grantmaking

Contact: spark@mamacash.org

Why the Spark Fund Is Different From Many Conventional Grants

Many funding programmes expect applicants to have:

  • Legal registration
  • Professional grant-writing capacity
  • A dedicated bank account
  • Formal governance structures
  • Paid staff
  • Large annual budgets

The Spark Fund deliberately reduces several of these barriers.

That makes it particularly valuable for activist groups whose political relevance may be high even though their institutional infrastructure is small.

Mama Cash’s model recognises that movements often begin as:

  • Informal collectives
  • Volunteer networks
  • Community initiatives
  • Newly organised campaigns

rather than formal NGOs.

The Fund is therefore designed to support activism at a stage when conventional donors may overlook it.

Conclusion

The Mama Cash Spark Fund 2026 offers grassroots feminist groups in the Netherlands and the ABCSSS islands an opportunity to receive between €5,000 and €12,000 for projects lasting up to two years.

The programme is particularly intended for self-led groups of women, girls, trans and intersex people working on urgent and contested political issues while pursuing structural and systemic change.

Mama Cash gives particular priority to organisations and collectives that have limited access to flexible funding, including informal or unregistered groups, newly established initiatives, volunteer-led groups and organisations with limited resources.

The Fund is especially accessible because applicants do not need to have an organisational bank account, official identification, a residence permit or formal registration as a foundation in order to apply.

Applications can be submitted in writing, by video or by audio, and can be completed in English or Dutch. Applicants needing another language can contact Mama Cash for possible accommodations.

Applications opened on 20 August 2026 and close on:

20 September 2026 at 11:59 PM CEST.

For grassroots groups led directly by communities affected by gender-based and intersectional inequality, the Spark Fund provides an unusually flexible pathway to fund bold feminist activism without requiring the conventional institutional structures expected by many grantmakers.

To know more about this opportunity, visit the official Mama Cash Spark Fund page.

item.content:encoded:
The Japan Society for the Promotion of Science (JSPS) Postdoctoral Fellowships for Research in Japan – Standard Program offers outstanding early-career researchers from around the world an opportunity to spend 12 to 24 months conducting collaborative research at universities and eligible research institutions in Japan.

The fellowship is one of Japan’s major international postdoctoral research programmes and is open across an exceptionally broad range of academic disciplines, including the humanities, social sciences and natural sciences. Successful Fellows work under the guidance of an eligible Japanese host researcher and join an established research environment in Japan while developing an international collaborative research project.

Financial support under the Standard Program includes a JPY 362,000 monthly maintenance allowance, a round-trip international air ticket under JSPS rules, a JPY 200,000 settling-in allowance, overseas travel insurance and access to a separate Grant-in-Aid for Scientific Research for eligible collaborative research expenses.

For FY2027, JSPS has scheduled two open-call recruitment rounds, with approximately 120 Fellowships planned in each round. The first round deadline was 28 August 2026 at 5:00 PM Japan Standard Time, while the second-round deadline is 23 April 2027 at 5:00 PM JST.

This deadline information is important because some third-party posts circulating online state that the application deadline is 15 November 2026. That date does not appear in the official JSPS FY2027 Standard Program open-call schedule. Applicants using an overseas nominating authority may face separate deadlines set by that nominating organization, but those deadlines vary by country and should not be presented as the universal JSPS deadline.

The official FY2027 Standard Program should therefore be understood as a host-based, highly competitive international postdoctoral fellowship, not a direct individual online application in which a researcher simply submits independently to JSPS.

Official programme information: JSPS Postdoctoral Fellowships for Research in Japan; JSPS International Fellowships for Research in Japan 2026

About the JSPS Postdoctoral Fellowships for Research in Japan

The Japan Society for the Promotion of Science operates several international fellowship programmes designed for researchers at different stages of their careers.

These include programmes for:

  • Pre-doctoral researchers
  • Postdoctoral researchers
  • Early-career researchers
  • Experienced international researchers
  • Short-term research visitors

The Standard Program, however, is specifically designed to give young overseas postdoctoral researchers an opportunity to conduct collaborative research with leading research groups at Japanese universities and other eligible research institutions.

The programme emphasizes genuine research collaboration rather than simply providing a researcher with funding to work independently.

Before an application is submitted, the overseas candidate and Japanese host researcher are expected to:

  • Establish contact
  • Develop a concrete research plan
  • Agree on the proposed collaboration
  • Identify an appropriate host institution
  • Demonstrate how the collaboration will advance the proposed research

These factors are explicitly considered during the JSPS selection process.

Fellowship Duration

The Standard Program runs for:

12 to 24 months.

This gives successful Fellows enough time to become meaningfully integrated into the host research environment rather than undertaking only a short academic visit.

Depending on the project, a Fellow may therefore spend:

  • One year
  • 18 months
  • Two years

conducting research in Japan.

The precise tenure is proposed through the application and should match the needs of the research collaboration.

FY2027 Number of Fellowships

The official FY2027 open-call schedule lists approximately:

120 Fellowship awards in the first recruitment round

and another:

120 Fellowship awards in the second recruitment round.

Therefore, the frequently advertised figure of “120 awards” is broadly correct for each FY2027 open-call recruitment round, rather than necessarily representing the total number of all Standard Program awards through every application route.

JSPS also receives Standard Program applications through overseas nominating authorities in selected countries and organisations.

FY2027 First Recruitment Round

The first FY2027 Standard Program open-call round had the following schedule:

Application deadline from host institution to JSPS:
28 August 2026 at 5:00 PM JST

Expected results:
Late December 2026

Permitted fellowship commencement period:
1 April 2027 to 30 September 2027

Approximate number of Fellowships:
120

As of September 2026, this first recruitment deadline has already passed.

FY2027 Second Recruitment Round

Researchers who missed the first round have another opportunity under the FY2027 Standard Program.

The second recruitment schedule is:

Application deadline from host institution to JSPS:
23 April 2027 at 5:00 PM JST

Expected results:
Early August 2027

Permitted fellowship commencement period:
1 September 2027 to 30 November 2027

Approximate number of Fellowships:
120

Prospective applicants should note that this is the deadline by which the Japanese host institution must submit the application to JSPS.

Universities may impose their own internal deadlines significantly earlier.

Candidates should therefore begin identifying a host researcher well in advance.

Important Clarification About the 15 November 2026 Deadline

A social-media version of this opportunity states:

15 November 2026

as the application deadline.

That date does not match the official FY2027 Standard Program open-call schedule published by JSPS.

The official deadlines are:

  • First round: 28 August 2026
  • Second round: 23 April 2027

However, JSPS also accepts some applications through overseas nominating authorities, and those organisations establish their own procedures and deadlines.

For this reason, a November deadline could potentially refer to a particular nomination route, but it should not be advertised as the general JSPS Standard Program deadline unless the relevant nominating authority specifically confirms it.

Difference Between the Standard Fellowship and Other JSPS Programmes

This distinction is particularly important because JSPS operates several programmes with different deadlines.

For example, the FY2027 Short-term Program (PE) currently has an official first-round deadline of:

25 September 2026 at 5:00 PM JST

and approximately 20 Fellowships are planned for that round.

That is a different programme.

The Short-term PE programme should not be confused with the:

Standard Program

which lasts 12–24 months and has approximately 120 places per FY2027 open-call round.

Fields of Research

One of the strongest features of the JSPS Standard Fellowship is its disciplinary breadth.

JSPS states that applications can be submitted in:

All fields of the humanities, social sciences and natural sciences.

This makes the fellowship relevant to researchers working across areas such as:

  • Anthropology
  • Archaeology
  • History
  • Languages
  • Literature
  • Philosophy
  • Political science
  • International relations
  • Economics
  • Sociology
  • Law
  • Education
  • Psychology
  • Mathematics
  • Physics
  • Chemistry
  • Engineering
  • Computer science
  • Informatics
  • Biology
  • Agriculture
  • Environmental sciences
  • Medicine
  • Dentistry
  • Pharmacy

The FY2027 review structure similarly covers disciplines including humanities, social sciences, mathematical and physical sciences, chemistry, engineering, informatics, biology, agriculture/environmental sciences, medicine, dentistry and pharmacy.

Who Is the Fellowship Designed For?

The Standard Program is intended for:

Young overseas postdoctoral researchers

who want to conduct collaborative research in Japan.

Applicants should normally be at an early stage after completing their doctorate.

The fellowship is not intended primarily for:

  • Undergraduate students
  • Master’s students
  • Researchers without an expected PhD by the fellowship start
  • Senior professors looking for short visiting appointments

Other JSPS programmes may serve some of those categories.

Doctoral Degree Requirement

For the Standard Program, an overseas candidate must normally have:

Obtained a doctoral degree within six years of the date the Fellowship begins

or:

Be expected to receive the PhD before the Fellowship begins.

The candidate’s employment status is not decisive.

JSPS explicitly states that whether the applicant currently holds a full-time position is not considered for this eligibility requirement.

This means applicants may potentially include:

  • Postdoctoral researchers
  • Research associates
  • Lecturers
  • Researchers between appointments
  • PhD candidates close to graduation

provided all other requirements are satisfied.

Applicants Who Have Not Yet Completed Their PhD

A candidate does not necessarily need to hold the doctorate when the application is submitted.

Researchers expected to obtain the doctoral degree before the Fellowship begins may apply.

If selected, they must submit documentation confirming the doctoral degree before their fellowship starts.

This can make the programme particularly valuable to final-stage PhD candidates planning the transition directly into postdoctoral research.

Maternity and Parental Leave Adjustment

JSPS also recognizes career interruptions connected with:

  • Maternity leave
  • Parental leave

The six-year post-PhD eligibility period can be adjusted by subtracting qualifying periods of maternity or parental leave when calculating the time elapsed since the doctorate was awarded.

This provision helps prevent researchers from being disadvantaged simply because they temporarily interrupted their academic careers for family responsibilities.

Nationality Requirement

Standard Program candidates must generally be citizens of a country that:

Has diplomatic relations with Japan.

JSPS also treats researchers from:

  • Taiwan
  • Palestine

as satisfying this requirement.

This makes the Standard Program broadly international.

It is therefore open to researchers from a very large number of countries across:

  • Africa
  • Asia
  • Europe
  • North America
  • Latin America and the Caribbean
  • Middle East
  • Oceania

provided the nationality requirement and all other eligibility conditions are satisfied.

Japanese Citizens and Permanent Residents

Persons who are:

  • Japanese citizens, or
  • Foreign nationals permitted permanent residence in Japan

are not eligible for the Standard Program under the published candidate rules.

The programme is specifically designed to bring overseas researchers into Japanese research institutions.

Previous JSPS Fellows

Applicants should also note an important restriction.

Researchers who previously received and started a Fellowship under the:

  • JSPS Postdoctoral Fellowship for Research in Japan – Standard
  • Pathway to University Positions in Japan

are not eligible again under the Standard Program.

Applicants who were previously selected but did not actually begin the Fellowship should consult the detailed eligibility rules applicable to their circumstances.

Financial Support

The JSPS Standard Fellowship provides an extensive support package intended to allow researchers to concentrate on their collaborative research in Japan.

The main components include:

  1. Monthly maintenance allowance
  2. International airfare
  3. Settling-in allowance
  4. Overseas travel insurance
  5. Potential research funding through KAKENHI

Monthly Maintenance Allowance

Standard Fellows receive:

JPY 362,000 per month.

For a 12-month Fellowship, that corresponds to approximately:

JPY 4,344,000 in maintenance allowances

before considering other benefits.

For a 24-month Fellowship, it would correspond to approximately:

JPY 8,688,000

at the currently published monthly rate.

The actual total received depends on the approved fellowship duration and programme rules.

Settling-In Allowance

Successful Fellows may receive a:

JPY 200,000 settling-in allowance.

This is intended to help with costs associated with beginning a temporary research stay in Japan.

Possible relocation-related costs can include:

  • Initial housing expenses
  • Essential household setup
  • Local transportation
  • Administrative arrangements

Applicants should follow the formal JSPS rules concerning eligible circumstances and payment.

Round-Trip International Airfare

JSPS provides:

A round-trip air ticket

in accordance with its programme regulations.

This considerably reduces the cost of relocating internationally for a long research fellowship.

However, candidates who are already living in Japan with a mailing address before the Fellowship starts are not entitled to the outbound airfare or settling-in allowance under the conditions described by JSPS.

Overseas Travel Insurance

The programme also includes:

Overseas travel insurance.

The specific coverage is governed by JSPS programme regulations.

Research Funding Through KAKENHI

In addition to the personal Fellowship support, a:

Grant-in-Aid for Scientific Research

may be available for cooperative research-related expenses.

The host researcher submits the research grant application through the Japanese host institution.

This research funding is separate from the Fellow’s:

  • Monthly maintenance allowance
  • Airfare
  • Settling-in allowance

and is intended to support the research project itself.

Is This a Fully Funded Fellowship?

The programme can reasonably be described as a fully funded postdoctoral research fellowship because it provides:

  • Monthly living support
  • International airfare
  • Relocation support
  • Insurance
  • Potential research funding

However, applicants should avoid interpreting “fully funded” as meaning that JSPS separately reimburses every possible personal expense.

The official terms of support should always govern financial expectations.

Is There an Application Fee?

JSPS’s official FY2027 Standard Program materials do not list an application fee as part of the normal open-call submission process.

The more important challenge is that applicants cannot simply apply independently.

They must build a relationship with an eligible host researcher and have the formal application submitted through the Japanese host institution.

How the Application Process Works

The Standard Program uses two principal application routes:

  1. Open Call through a Japanese host institution
  2. Nomination through an approved overseas nominating authority

These routes should not be confused because their procedures and deadlines can differ.

Route 1: Open Call Through a Japanese Host Researcher

For the open call, the overseas researcher first needs to identify:

An eligible researcher in Japan willing to serve as host.

That host researcher then becomes the formal applicant in the JSPS system.

JSPS states that the application is made through the:

Japanese host institution

using the JSPS Electronic Application System.

The overseas candidate therefore cannot simply submit the complete application independently to JSPS.

Why Finding a Host Researcher Is Crucial

The relationship between candidate and host is central to the selection process.

JSPS expects the two researchers to have:

  • Established contact before applying
  • Created a concrete research plan
  • Identified the value of the collaboration

A weak application based only on the prestige of the overseas candidate is therefore unlikely to be enough.

The proposal needs to explain why conducting the research with this particular Japanese researcher and institution adds value.

Who Can Serve as a Host Researcher?

The host researcher generally needs to be affiliated with an institution eligible under Japan’s KAKENHI framework.

Eligible institutions include categories such as:

  • Universities
  • Inter-university research institutes
  • MEXT-affiliated research institutions
  • Colleges of technology
  • Other institutions designated by the Minister of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology

The host researcher normally needs to be eligible to apply for KAKENHI funding and capable of providing an appropriate research environment for the overseas Fellow.

Host Researchers Can Submit Several Applications

Each eligible Japanese host researcher can submit up to:

Three applications

under the programme.

Where the host submits applications for more than one candidate at the same time, priorities must be indicated.

Prospective Fellows should therefore discuss the host’s application situation clearly before beginning substantial proposal preparation.

Route 2: Overseas Nominating Authorities

JSPS also accepts Standard Program candidates through approved:

Overseas nominating authorities.

The list includes organisations in countries such as:

  • Australia
  • Austria
  • Belgium
  • Bulgaria
  • Canada
  • Czech Republic
  • Estonia
  • France
  • Germany
  • Hungary
  • Italy
  • New Zealand
  • Poland
  • Slovakia
  • Slovenia
  • Sweden
  • Switzerland
  • United Kingdom
  • Ukraine
  • United States

as well as the United Nations University.

Candidates using this route need to contact the relevant authority directly because:

Application procedures and deadlines are determined by the nominating authority.

This is another reason not to publish one third-party deadline as though it applies universally.

Required Application Materials

The FY2027 application page provides separate forms completed by the:

  • Japanese host researcher
  • Foreign candidate
  • Recommender

The candidate completes Form 2, while the host researcher completes the information submitted through the JSPS Electronic Application System.

A recommendation letter is also required and may be written in:

  • English
  • Japanese

Applicants should download the current FY2027 materials rather than reusing forms from an earlier year.

Selection Process

Applications under the Standard open-call route undergo a:

Two-stage competitive review process.

The stages are:

  1. Document review
  2. Panel review

The evaluation is undertaken by the JSPS International Program Committee, consisting of researchers in Japan.

Six Examiners Review Each Application

During the initial document-review stage:

Six examiners review each application.

Experts are assigned according to the research field.

Applications are scored on a five-point scale:

  • 5 – Superlative
  • 4 – Excellent
  • 3 – Good
  • 2 – Fair
  • 1 – Poor

The averaged document-review score becomes an important basis for determining which applications progress through panel review.

What Reviewers Evaluate

Reviewers consider factors such as:

  • Research achievements
  • Quality of the research plan
  • Estimated research capacity
  • Future potential
  • Ability to establish new research networks

This means candidates should not treat the application as simply another academic CV competition.

The proposal itself matters substantially.

Importance of the Proposed Collaboration

JSPS explicitly wants the collaboration to contribute to:

  • Advancement of science in Japan
  • Advancement of science internationally
  • Development of the proposed field
  • The candidate’s research
  • The host researcher’s research

The proposal should therefore explain:

Why does this research need to be conducted collaboratively in Japan?

A strong answer to that question is essential.

Diversity in Selection

JSPS also states that it seeks, as far as possible, to avoid excessive concentration of selected Fellows by:

  • Nationality
  • Host institution
  • Area of specialization

and seeks to enable researchers from a diverse range of countries to come to Japan.

There is nevertheless no country quota guaranteeing selection.

How Competitive Is the Fellowship?

The Standard Program is highly competitive.

For the FY2026 first recruitment round, JSPS reported:

  • 1,868 applications
  • 145 selected Fellows
  • 7.8% selection rate

For the second FY2026 recruitment:

  • 2,231 applications
  • 125 selected Fellows
  • 5.6% selection rate

These historical figures demonstrate that meeting the eligibility criteria alone is far from sufficient.

Applicants need a strong research record, convincing host relationship and carefully designed research proposal.

Preparing a Competitive Application

1. Start by Finding the Right Japanese Host

Do not approach the host search as an administrative formality.

Look for researchers whose work genuinely intersects with yours.

Review:

  • Recent publications
  • Current projects
  • Research group expertise
  • Available facilities
  • Institutional strengths

Then explain specifically why collaboration would create research value.

2. Contact Hosts Early

The official JSPS deadline is not necessarily your practical deadline.

The sequence usually involves:

candidate → host researcher → host institution → JSPS.

Japanese universities may establish internal application deadlines weeks or even more than a month before the JSPS deadline.

Beginning host outreach only shortly before April 23, 2027 would therefore be risky.

3. Build a Concrete Research Plan

JSPS explicitly evaluates whether the candidate and host have developed a concrete collaborative plan.

A strong proposal should explain:

  • Research question
  • Academic significance
  • Methodology
  • Research schedule
  • Host institution resources
  • Division of collaboration
  • Expected outcomes
  • International significance

4. Explain Why Japan Is Necessary

Avoid a proposal that could be conducted anywhere.

Identify what Japan offers that is specifically relevant, such as:

  • Unique archives
  • Laboratories
  • Datasets
  • Research facilities
  • Field sites
  • Intellectual traditions
  • Technical expertise
  • Host research network

This strengthens the logic behind the Fellowship.

5. Show Future Research Potential

The fellowship is intended for early-career researchers.

Reviewers therefore consider not only what candidates have already accomplished but also their:

Future potential.

Your proposal should demonstrate how the fellowship will help build:

  • A coherent academic trajectory
  • New international collaboration
  • Future publications
  • Sustainable research networks
  • New methodological expertise

6. Highlight Research Achievements Strategically

Your publication list matters, but quantity alone is not enough.

Prioritize evidence demonstrating:

  • Research independence
  • Scholarly quality
  • Relevance to the proposed project
  • Ability to complete ambitious research

Applicants from fields where journal publication is less dominant should present the strongest appropriate research outputs in their discipline.

FY2027 Timeline at a Glance

Recruitment JSPS deadline Results Fellowship start window Planned awards
First FY2027 Standard round 28 August 2026, 5 PM JST Late December 2026 1 April–30 September 2027 120
Second FY2027 Standard round 23 April 2027, 5 PM JST Early August 2027 1 September–30 November 2027 120

Remember that these are host institution-to-JSPS deadlines.

Internal university deadlines may occur earlier.

Key Fellowship Benefits at a Glance

Programme: JSPS Postdoctoral Fellowships for Research in Japan – Standard

Country: Japan

Research level: Postdoctoral

Fields: Humanities, social sciences and natural sciences

Duration: 12–24 months

Monthly maintenance allowance: JPY 362,000

Settling-in allowance: JPY 200,000

International airfare: Round-trip ticket under JSPS rules

Insurance: Overseas travel insurance

Research expenses: Separate Grant-in-Aid may be available

FY2027 awards: Approximately 120 in each open-call recruitment round

Next official FY2027 Standard open-call deadline: 23 April 2027 at 5:00 PM JST

Official Application Links

Main JSPS international fellowship portal:

JSPS International Fellowships for Research in Japan

Standard Program:

JSPS Postdoctoral Fellowship Standard Program

FY2027 application forms and guidance:

FY2027 JSPS Application Guidelines

FY2027 Standard Program schedule:

FY2027 Standard Fellowship Application Schedule

Conclusion

The JSPS Postdoctoral Fellowship for Research in Japan 2027 – Standard Program is one of the most substantial opportunities available to early-career international researchers seeking to build a sustained research collaboration in Japan.

The programme is open across the humanities, social sciences and natural sciences and offers 12 to 24 months of support, including a JPY 362,000 monthly maintenance allowance, JPY 200,000 settling-in allowance, round-trip international airfare and overseas travel insurance, with separate research funding potentially available through KAKENHI.

Candidates must generally be nationals of countries with diplomatic relations with Japan, with Taiwan and Palestine treated as eligible for this purpose, and must have obtained their doctorate within the relevant six-year period or be expected to receive their PhD before the Fellowship begins. Japanese citizens and permanent residents of Japan are not eligible under the Standard overseas-researcher programme.

The application process is built around collaboration. Candidates need an eligible Japanese host researcher and a concrete research plan, and open-call applications are submitted through the host institution rather than directly by the overseas candidate.

For FY2027, JSPS plans approximately 120 Standard Fellowships in each of two open-call rounds. The first deadline was 28 August 2026, while the second-round host-institution deadline is 23 April 2027 at 5:00 PM JST.

Applicants should therefore disregard claims that 15 November 2026 is the universal Standard Fellowship deadline unless that date comes from a specific overseas nominating authority relevant to them.

For researchers who can develop a strong partnership with a Japanese host and articulate a compelling collaborative project, the JSPS Standard Fellowship offers substantial financial support, international research exposure and the opportunity to build long-term academic networks in Japan.

Key Summary: The I AM NALA Fellowship 2027 is inviting applications from young African women aged 18–40 who are refugees, internally displaced, stateless, or displaced in the diaspora and are aspiring or current political leaders. The fully supported fellowship runs from January to July 2027, with capacity-building, mentorship, technical support, solidarity, networking and leadership opportunities. Application deadline: 31 October 2026.

I AM NALA Fellowship 2027

Nalafem has opened applications for the I AM NALA Fellowship Programme 2027, a leadership initiative designed to support young African women affected by displacement and insecurity who are playing or seeking to play meaningful roles in political leadership, peacebuilding and decision-making.

The fellowship will run from January 2027 to July 2027 and will engage 20 young women political leaders from across Africa, including displaced Africans in the diaspora.

The programme is particularly focused on women who have been displaced because of political or climate-related crises and insecurity.

Important: Applicants who are not refugees, internally displaced, displaced or stateless will not be considered.

Who Can Apply for the I AM NALA Fellowship?

The fellowship is looking for young African women aged 18–40 who demonstrate leadership and engagement in political, social justice, peacebuilding or advocacy efforts.

Applicants may include:

  • Leaders of a campaign or women’s group
  • Members of an existing consortium or collective focused on alliance building
  • Young women involved in cross-conflict negotiations
  • Young women politicians currently serving in political office
  • Aspiring or current political leaders working on issues aligned with the Africa Young Women Beijing +25 Manifesto demands. We are looking for political leaders in one or more of the Africa Young Women Beijing +25 Manifesto demands and who embrace Nalafem Values

Applicants should also demonstrate an understanding of and commitment to Nalafem’s values, including:

  • Solidarity
  • Social Justice
  • Dignity
  • Equity
  • Decolonial Feminist Pan-Africanism

What Does the Fellowship Offer?

The I AM NALA Fellowship is designed to strengthen the leadership capacity of displaced and stateless African women who can contribute to political and peacebuilding processes.

Fellows will receive access to:

  • Capacity-building and technical support
  • Mentorship from experienced leaders and experts
  • Leadership development
  • Solidarity and networking opportunities
  • Access to resources
  • Training and masterclasses
  • Opportunities to participate in dialogues with senior leaders and experienced practitioners
  • Potential in-person engagements

The fellowship will include bi-monthly online sessions, providing fellows with opportunities to learn alongside mentors and experts from a range of institutions and organisations.

Who Is the Fellowship For?

The programme is specifically intended for refugee, internally displaced, displaced and stateless young African women, including displaced Africans living in the diaspora.

The fellowship seeks women who have the potential to contribute to:

  • Political negotiations
  • Decision-making
  • Democratic transitions
  • Reconciliation
  • Peacebuilding
  • Political leadership
  • Advocacy and social justice
  • Conflict resolution

The programme therefore provides an opportunity for young women whose experiences of displacement have shaped their leadership and who are positioned to contribute to positive change in their countries of origin or host countries.

I AM NALA Fellowship 2027 Deadline

The application deadline is:

📅 31 October 2026

Only shortlisted candidates will be contacted, with notifications expected by:

📅 6 November 2026

The fellowship itself is scheduled to take place from:

📅 January 2027 – July 2027

How to Apply

Interested applicants should complete the full I AM NALA Fellowship application form before the deadline.

Young African women aged 18–40 who are refugees, internally displaced, displaced or stateless and demonstrate leadership or engagement in political, advocacy, peacebuilding or related initiatives.

No. The organisers explicitly state that applications from people who are not refugees, IDPs, displaced or stateless will not be considered.

When does the 2027 fellowship take place?
The fellowship is scheduled for January 2027 to July 2027.

The programme will engage 20 young women political leaders from Africa, including displaced Africans in the diaspora.
